screens.title: First Boot: Install Raspberry Pi OS and Complete Initial Setup
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you will learn how to prepare a Raspberry Pi for first use by installing Raspberry Pi OS, configuring essential settings before the first boot, and finishing initial configuration on the device itself. We focus on a repeatable process: use the Raspberry Pi Imager to write the image, set a hostname, create credentials, and provide Wi‑Fi and SSH details so the board can boot headless. You will also learn how the first boot expands the filesystem and when the setup wizard runs. Finally, we introduce raspi-config, the built‑in configuration tool you will use to enable interfaces such as SPI, I2C, UART, and the camera, and to change locales and other system settings. This matters because a correctly prepared microSD card and a clean initial setup make later hardware projects and remote connections reliable and secure. As you go, watch for two common pitfalls: relying on an old default username and forgetting to enable SSH or provide Wi‑Fi for headless setups. By the end you will know which OS image to pick, what preconfiguration saves time, and how to make remote access safe and repeatable. Ready to begin?

screens.title: Raspberry Pi OS: Desktop vs Lite, 32‑bit vs 64‑bit
screens.narratorSegment: Raspberry Pi OS comes in multiple variants and picking the right one matters for available features and resource use. Desktop images include a graphical environment and recommended software, making them a good fit if you will attach a monitor or want a familiar desktop experience. The Lite image has no graphical interface and is intentionally minimal; it's ideal for headless servers, automation scripts, and projects where every megabyte of storage and memory matters. Another important choice is 32‑bit versus 64‑bit. A 32‑bit image can run on all Pi models and may be slightly more compatible with older software packages. A 64‑bit image can address more memory and can improve performance for workloads that benefit from 64‑bit arithmetic, but it is useful only when your hardware and required software support it. As a concrete example, choose Desktop 64‑bit if you plan to run a GUI desktop with heavier applications on a recent Pi model. Choose Lite 32‑bit for a headless sensor logger that only needs SSH. A common misconception is that Desktop is always better; in fact, a Desktop image can add unnecessary overhead for simple headless projects. Takeaway: match the image to your use case — GUI needs, memory demands, and whether you'll operate headless — and you will avoid wasted space and performance surprises.

screens.title: Install with Raspberry Pi Imager
screens.narratorSegment: The Raspberry Pi Imager is the simplest, most reliable way to put Raspberry Pi OS onto a microSD card. The typical process begins by installing Imager on your computer, inserting a microSD card in a reader, and opening Imager. Then select the target device — choose the Raspberry Pi model you will use — and pick the OS image, for example the recommended 64‑bit Desktop or the Lite variant. Select the microSD card as storage. Before you click Write, use the settings or gear icon to preconfigure options: set a hostname like raspberrypi. local, create a unique username and a strong password, add Wi‑Fi SSID and password for your network, choose locale and keyboard layout, and enable SSH if you plan to connect remotely. After confirming these options, start the write process and wait. Imager downloads and writes the image, then verifies it. When it completes, eject the microSD card safely. A concrete example: preconfigure Wi‑Fi and SSH so the Pi can boot headless and accept a remote connection immediately. A common mistake is skipping preconfiguration and then trying to access a headless Pi with no network credentials set. Key takeaway: use Imager’s settings to automate repetitive choices and avoid first‑boot surprises.

screens.title: Preparing microSD and Hardware
screens.narratorSegment: A stable microSD card and a reliable card reader are foundational to a successful Raspberry Pi setup. Choose a card with enough capacity for your projects and a reasonable speed class; slow or failing cards cause intermittent errors. Use a USB card reader if your computer lacks a built‑in slot, and confirm the operating system detects the card before running Imager. When Imager finishes writing and verifying the image, always use the operating system’s safe eject option — removing the card prematurely can corrupt the filesystem. Insert the card into the Pi firmly, connect power after display and peripherals or ensure network preconfiguration for headless boot. A concrete example: if you intend to run a small server with logging, select a 16GB or larger card with higher endurance to reduce wear. A common misconception is that any cheap card will work; in practice, low-quality cards fail sooner and cause confusing boot errors. If a Pi fails to boot, reinsert the card into a computer and check that the boot partition is present and that Imager completed the verification step successfully. Takeaway: good physical preparation prevents elusive failures and saves time when you move from writing images to doing real projects.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.4 › microSD & Hardware
Card & Reader Checklist
  • Choose capacity and endurance appropriate for your project (logs, OS, apps).
  • Use a compatible and reliable USB card reader if necessary.
  • Confirm the system detects the card before writing the image.
  • After writing, allow verification to finish and use safe eject.
Boot Prep
Insert the prepared microSD card into the Raspberry Pi, connect power, and let the first boot complete. If you preconfigured Wi‑Fi and SSH, you can boot headless and connect remotely.
Example
Use a 16GB high‑endurance card for a small server to reduce wear and risk of corruption.
Pitfall
Removing the card before verification finishes can damage the filesystem; always safe eject first.
Key Takeaway

Choose quality cards and complete the write+verify cycle. Physical prep avoids most mysterious boot failures.

screens.title: Pre-configuration Options in Imager
screens.narratorSegment: Raspberry Pi Imager’s pre‑configuration options let you automate key setup steps so the Pi is ready right after the first boot. Hostname defines the device’s network name — for example, raspberrypi. local — which makes it easier to find the Pi on your local network. Creating a unique username and strong password replaces the old default account and improves security. Wi‑Fi SSID and password added in Imager allow a headless Pi to join your network and be reachable immediately. Locale settings like timezone and keyboard layout ensure your shell and applications show the right formats. Enabling SSH provides remote shell access so you can manage the device from another computer. A concrete example: set hostname to a descriptive name such as "sensor-station-01", create a secure account dedicated to that task, and add your network credentials so the board boots and you can SSH in without a monitor. A common mistake is believing the old default username is still automatically present; modern Imager expects you to create the account during preconfiguration. Takeaway: preconfigure these settings to reduce friction, improve security, and support headless workflows right away.

keyIdea.text: Using Imager’s settings to set hostname, credentials, Wi‑Fi, locale, and SSH produces a ready-to-use Pi on first boot and lowers setup friction.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.4 › Pre-configuration
Settings Explained
Hostname: Network name for discovery and SSH connections.
Username & Password: Create a unique account instead of using legacy defaults.
Wi‑Fi: SSID and passphrase so the Pi can join your network on first boot.
Locale: Timezone and keyboard to ensure regional formats are correct.
SSH: Enable remote shell access for headless operation.
Example & Pitfall
Example: Set hostname to sensor-station-01, create a distinct user, and prefill Wi‑Fi so you can SSH in as soon as the Pi boots. Pitfall: skipping username creation and relying on an assumed default can lock you out.
Why it matters
Preconfiguration avoids manual keyboard input and speeds repeatable device provisioning.
Security note
Always choose a strong password and a unique username; do not leave default or predictable credentials.
Key Takeaway

Preconfigure hostname, credentials, Wi‑Fi, locale, and SSH to create a ready and secure device from first boot.

screens.title: Writing the Image and Verifying
screens.narratorSegment: After selecting the image and configuring settings in Imager, begin the write process. Imager will download the image if needed, write it to the microSD card, and run a verification step to check the integrity of the written data. Allow the entire sequence to finish; interruption during write or verification can produce a corrupted installation and a Pi that fails to boot. When Imager signals completion, use the operating system’s eject or unmount action before removing the card from the reader. Insert the microSD card into the Pi only after it is fully written and ejected. A concrete scenario: you prepare a headless node, start the write, and leave the machine to finish; verify success notification before ejection. A common misconception is that you can remove the card as soon as the progress bar reaches 100 percent; the subsequent verification step matters and finishes later. If verification fails, do not try to reuse the card immediately — reformat and repeat the write from Imager or try a different card. Takeaway: writing plus verification and safe-eject are necessary steps to ensure a reliable bootable microSD card.

keyIdea.title: Write + Verify + Eject
keyIdea.text: Allow Imager to complete writing and verification, then safely eject the microSD card to prevent filesystem corruption.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.4 › Write & Verify
Write Process
Imager downloads the OS image if needed, writes it to the selected microSD card, and verifies the written data. Do not interrupt these steps.
Start Write
Begin only after confirming device and OS selection.
Verify
Wait for verification to ensure integrity; progress bars may not reflect final verification completion.
Safe Eject
Use your OS eject or unmount action before removing the card to avoid corruption.
Example scenario
Start the write on your workstation and walk away; return when Imager shows completion and then safely eject the card.
Common mistake
Removing the card immediately after the progress bar reaches 100% can leave verification incomplete and create a non-bootable card.
Key Takeaway

Let Imager finish writing and verifying, then eject safely. Verification protects against corrupted installations.

screens.title: First Boot and the Setup Wizard
screens.narratorSegment: When you power the Raspberry Pi with a prepared microSD card, the first boot does two things: it expands the filesystem to use the full card and it runs initial configuration tasks. If you used Imager to preconfigure hostname, Wi‑Fi, and SSH, many setup steps are already satisfied and the graphical setup wizard may skip those items. If you have a monitor and keyboard attached, the Pi will show the desktop or the setup wizard prompting for country, language, timezone, and password if not already set. For headless setups, you should be able to connect over SSH once the board is on the network, using the username and hostname you configured. A concrete example: a Pi with preconfigured Wi‑Fi will join the network and accept SSH connections, letting you complete any remaining local setup remotely. A common misconception is that the setup wizard always runs and requires manual input; it will skip or reduce prompts if preconfiguration is present. If the Pi takes longer than a minute or two, be patient — expanding the filesystem and background configuration can take extra time on first boot. Takeaway: first boot both prepares the filesystem and respects preconfigured values, enabling headless workflows when done correctly.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.4 › First Boot
What Happens on First Boot
The system expands the filesystem to use the entire microSD card and applies configuration tasks. If preconfiguration was provided, such as Wi‑Fi and SSH, the wizard may skip those prompts.
Filesystem Expand
Ensures the OS can use all available space on the card.
Setup Wizard
Guides locale choices and password setup if not preconfigured.
Headless Access
With Wi‑Fi and SSH prefilled, the Pi joins your network and is reachable remotely.
Example
Preconfigured Pi boots headless and accepts SSH under the configured username at the configured hostname.
Common misconception
Believing the setup wizard always requires manual input — it will skip prompts if you already provided values via Imager.
Key Takeaway

First boot readies the filesystem and applies configured options, enabling GUI or headless workflows depending on what you prepared.

screens.title: Connecting via SSH
screens.narratorSegment: SSH provides a secure shell into your Raspberry Pi and is the usual way to manage a headless device. After the Pi joins your network, open a terminal on your computer and connect using the SSH command syntax followed by the username and hostname — for example, connect to username at raspberrypi. local. The first time you connect you will be asked to accept the host fingerprint; type yes to continue and enter your password when prompted. Once logged in, verify the OS with the system information command that shows distribution name and version, confirming the image you expected is installed. As a concrete example, connect as the user you created during Imager preconfiguration and run the version check to confirm Desktop or Lite and bitness. A common misconception is that SSH must be enabled in the GUI; in fact you can pre-enable SSH in Imager or enable it later with raspi-config. Security note: use strong passwords and consider disabling password authentication in favor of keys for long-term deployments. Takeaway: SSH gives you immediate remote shell access; accept the fingerprint once, authenticate, then confirm the OS version to ensure the correct image was installed.

keyIdea.title: SSH Access
keyIdea.text: SSH allows secure remote management. Verify host fingerprint, authenticate with credentials, and confirm the OS version after login.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.4 › SSH Connection
SSH Walkthrough
Open a terminal on your computer. Connect to the Pi using the SSH command with the username and hostname you configured. Accept the fingerprint when prompted and enter your password to authenticate.
What to expect
Prompt to accept host fingerprint once, then a password prompt. After login, you have a shell to run commands and verify system details.
Key Takeaway

Use SSH to manage a headless Pi. Confirm the OS version after login to ensure the correct image was installed.

Example Command
ssh username@raspberrypi.local

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson you will learn how to prepare a Raspberry Pi for first use by installing Raspberry Pi OS, configuring essential settings before the first boot, and finishing initial configuration on the device itself. We focus on a repeatable process: use the Raspberry Pi Imager to write the image, set a hostname, create credentials, and provide Wi‑Fi and SSH details so the board can boot headless. You will also learn how the first boot expands the filesystem and when the setup wizard runs. Finally, we introduce raspi-config, the built‑in configuration tool you will use to enable interfaces such as SPI, I2C, UART, and the camera, and to change locales and other system settings. This matters because a correctly prepared microSD card and a clean initial setup make later hardware projects and remote connections reliable and secure. As you go, watch for two common pitfalls: relying on an old default username and forgetting to enable SSH or provide Wi‑Fi for headless setups. By the end you will know which OS image to pick, what preconfiguration saves time, and how to make remote access safe and repeatable. Ready to begin?

By the end of this chapter you'll perform a complete initial setup of a Raspberry Pi. First, you will write the Raspberry Pi OS image to a microSD card using Raspberry Pi Imager and understand the difference between Desktop and Lite images as applied to your project. Next, you will preconfigure essential details in Imager: set a hostname, create a unique username and strong password, and enter Wi‑Fi credentials so the board can boot without a monitor. You will also enable SSH for remote access when needed. After booting the Pi you will complete any remaining setup steps and confirm the OS is correct. Finally, you will use raspi-config to enable interfaces like SPI, I2C, UART, and the camera, and know when a reboot is required. Each skill reduces friction on later hardware work and improves security. Practice these steps to make future projects repeatable and easier to troubleshoot.

This second objectives screen highlights how the skills are used in practice. Installing the correct Raspberry Pi OS image matters because Desktop versions include graphical tools while Lite is lean and suited to headless servers. Preconfiguring hostname and Wi‑Fi in Imager removes the need for a screen or keyboard and prevents you from being locked out. Enabling SSH before first boot is a tiny step that gives you immediate remote shell access and saves time. Using raspi-config to turn on interfaces is important when you attach sensors, cameras, or serial devices; many interface changes need a reboot to activate. Practicing these steps makes later experiments with hardware or network services straightforward and repeatable. Keep in mind the common misconception that the old default username is still used; you should always create a new username during preconfiguration to maintain security.

Raspberry Pi OS comes in multiple variants and picking the right one matters for available features and resource use. Desktop images include a graphical environment and recommended software, making them a good fit if you will attach a monitor or want a familiar desktop experience. The Lite image has no graphical interface and is intentionally minimal; it's ideal for headless servers, automation scripts, and projects where every megabyte of storage and memory matters. Another important choice is 32‑bit versus 64‑bit. A 32‑bit image can run on all Pi models and may be slightly more compatible with older software packages. A 64‑bit image can address more memory and can improve performance for workloads that benefit from 64‑bit arithmetic, but it is useful only when your hardware and required software support it. As a concrete example, choose Desktop 64‑bit if you plan to run a GUI desktop with heavier applications on a recent Pi model. Choose Lite 32‑bit for a headless sensor logger that only needs SSH. A common misconception is that Desktop is always better; in fact, a Desktop image can add unnecessary overhead for simple headless projects. Takeaway: match the image to your use case — GUI needs, memory demands, and whether you'll operate headless — and you will avoid wasted space and performance surprises.

The Raspberry Pi Imager is the simplest, most reliable way to put Raspberry Pi OS onto a microSD card. The typical process begins by installing Imager on your computer, inserting a microSD card in a reader, and opening Imager. Then select the target device — choose the Raspberry Pi model you will use — and pick the OS image, for example the recommended 64‑bit Desktop or the Lite variant. Select the microSD card as storage. Before you click Write, use the settings or gear icon to preconfigure options: set a hostname like raspberrypi. local, create a unique username and a strong password, add Wi‑Fi SSID and password for your network, choose locale and keyboard layout, and enable SSH if you plan to connect remotely. After confirming these options, start the write process and wait. Imager downloads and writes the image, then verifies it. When it completes, eject the microSD card safely. A concrete example: preconfigure Wi‑Fi and SSH so the Pi can boot headless and accept a remote connection immediately. A common mistake is skipping preconfiguration and then trying to access a headless Pi with no network credentials set. Key takeaway: use Imager’s settings to automate repetitive choices and avoid first‑boot surprises.

A stable microSD card and a reliable card reader are foundational to a successful Raspberry Pi setup. Choose a card with enough capacity for your projects and a reasonable speed class; slow or failing cards cause intermittent errors. Use a USB card reader if your computer lacks a built‑in slot, and confirm the operating system detects the card before running Imager. When Imager finishes writing and verifying the image, always use the operating system’s safe eject option — removing the card prematurely can corrupt the filesystem. Insert the card into the Pi firmly, connect power after display and peripherals or ensure network preconfiguration for headless boot. A concrete example: if you intend to run a small server with logging, select a 16GB or larger card with higher endurance to reduce wear. A common misconception is that any cheap card will work; in practice, low-quality cards fail sooner and cause confusing boot errors. If a Pi fails to boot, reinsert the card into a computer and check that the boot partition is present and that Imager completed the verification step successfully. Takeaway: good physical preparation prevents elusive failures and saves time when you move from writing images to doing real projects.

Raspberry Pi Imager’s pre‑configuration options let you automate key setup steps so the Pi is ready right after the first boot. Hostname defines the device’s network name — for example, raspberrypi. local — which makes it easier to find the Pi on your local network. Creating a unique username and strong password replaces the old default account and improves security. Wi‑Fi SSID and password added in Imager allow a headless Pi to join your network and be reachable immediately. Locale settings like timezone and keyboard layout ensure your shell and applications show the right formats. Enabling SSH provides remote shell access so you can manage the device from another computer. A concrete example: set hostname to a descriptive name such as "sensor-station-01", create a secure account dedicated to that task, and add your network credentials so the board boots and you can SSH in without a monitor. A common mistake is believing the old default username is still automatically present; modern Imager expects you to create the account during preconfiguration. Takeaway: preconfigure these settings to reduce friction, improve security, and support headless workflows right away.

After selecting the image and configuring settings in Imager, begin the write process. Imager will download the image if needed, write it to the microSD card, and run a verification step to check the integrity of the written data. Allow the entire sequence to finish; interruption during write or verification can produce a corrupted installation and a Pi that fails to boot. When Imager signals completion, use the operating system’s eject or unmount action before removing the card from the reader. Insert the microSD card into the Pi only after it is fully written and ejected. A concrete scenario: you prepare a headless node, start the write, and leave the machine to finish; verify success notification before ejection. A common misconception is that you can remove the card as soon as the progress bar reaches 100 percent; the subsequent verification step matters and finishes later. If verification fails, do not try to reuse the card immediately — reformat and repeat the write from Imager or try a different card. Takeaway: writing plus verification and safe-eject are necessary steps to ensure a reliable bootable microSD card.

When you power the Raspberry Pi with a prepared microSD card, the first boot does two things: it expands the filesystem to use the full card and it runs initial configuration tasks. If you used Imager to preconfigure hostname, Wi‑Fi, and SSH, many setup steps are already satisfied and the graphical setup wizard may skip those items. If you have a monitor and keyboard attached, the Pi will show the desktop or the setup wizard prompting for country, language, timezone, and password if not already set. For headless setups, you should be able to connect over SSH once the board is on the network, using the username and hostname you configured. A concrete example: a Pi with preconfigured Wi‑Fi will join the network and accept SSH connections, letting you complete any remaining local setup remotely. A common misconception is that the setup wizard always runs and requires manual input; it will skip or reduce prompts if preconfiguration is present. If the Pi takes longer than a minute or two, be patient — expanding the filesystem and background configuration can take extra time on first boot. Takeaway: first boot both prepares the filesystem and respects preconfigured values, enabling headless workflows when done correctly.

SSH provides a secure shell into your Raspberry Pi and is the usual way to manage a headless device. After the Pi joins your network, open a terminal on your computer and connect using the SSH command syntax followed by the username and hostname — for example, connect to username at raspberrypi. local. The first time you connect you will be asked to accept the host fingerprint; type yes to continue and enter your password when prompted. Once logged in, verify the OS with the system information command that shows distribution name and version, confirming the image you expected is installed. As a concrete example, connect as the user you created during Imager preconfiguration and run the version check to confirm Desktop or Lite and bitness.
